families.skill: turn a condition around from counts
families.prompt: Of {tot} {who} checked, {ip} are {bad}. The test is positive for {a} of the {bad} {who} and for {b} of the rest. What is $P(\text{{{bad}}} \mid +)$? Give a fraction.

wrong.line: That is $P(+ \mid \text{{{bad}}})$: you divided by the {ip} {bad} {who}. Given a positive, divide by all {pos} positives.
You divided by all {tot} {who}. Given a positive, only the {pos} positives are left.

solution: Every positive is one of the {a} {bad} {who} or one of the {b} others: ${a} + {b} = {pos}$ positives.
So $P(\text{{{bad}}} \mid +) = \tfrac{{{a}}}{{{pos}}}$, which is ${key:frac}$ in lowest terms.

families.skill: turn a condition around from rates
families.prompt: {pp}% of {who} are {bad}. The test is positive for {s}% of {bad} {who} and {f}% of the others. What is $P(\text{{{bad}}} \mid +)$, to 3 decimal places?

wrong.line: That is $P(+ \mid \text{{{bad}}})$, the other way round. Put the {bad}-and-positive path over every positive path.
That is $P(\text{{{bad}}} \cap +)$. Divide it by $P(+)$, every path into a positive.
You added {fd} for the others without weighting it by their share, {q}.

families.skill: add every path into the evidence
families.prompt: {pp}% of {who} are {bad}. The test is positive for {s}% of {bad} {who} and {f}% of the others. What is $P(+)$, the chance a random one tests positive?

wrong.line: That is only the {bad}-and-positive path. A positive can also come from the others: add ${q} \times {fd}$.
You added {fd} for the others without weighting it by their share, {q}.

solution: The {bad}-and-positive path is ${p} \times {sd} = {j}$. The other positive path is ${q} \times {fd} = {fp}$.
